grants.notes:
SCOPE AND METHOD. Everything below was read from the DEV database (oqermaidggvanahumjmj) via pg_policy/pg_class/pg_proc, not inferred from app code. Read-only; nothing was written. 356 policies across 113 tables in public; 0 RESTRICTIVE policies (all permissive, so within a command the branches OR together); 38 policies target PUBLIC (polroles = {0}) rather than `authenticated` — for those, anon is technically in scope but every expression resolves false for a caller with no users row.

HOW TO READ THE TABLE ENTRIES.
- grantKeys "@name:action" = expand via the helpers array (helper grantKeys are module ids; append ":"+action). "@name" with no action = the helper's key list is already action-qualified.
- grantKeys [] + extraConditions [] + predictable true => UNCONDITIONALLY ALLOWED for any authenticated user (a literal `true` policy).
- extraConditions containing "NO POLICY — denied" => no policy exists for that command; denied for authenticated regardless of grants.
- predictableFromGrantsAlone=false => grant-necessary-but-not-sufficient (or grant-irrelevant): the cell needs the visibility dial, an owner/identity comparison, a department string, a parent-row visibility check, or a jsonb field match.

E15 SWEEP RESULT (the thing you asked me to check). Still exactly THREE literal-NULL-owner policies, all three on billing_line_items (select, update, delete). NO second instance appeared anywhere else in the schema. I swept with `pg_get_expr(...) ~* 'NULL::(text|character)'` over both polqual and polwithcheck across all 356 policies, which is broader than the LIKE used for G7. Confirmed unchanged.

BROADER OBSERVATIONS FROM THE SWEEP (verified in the DB, several are new relative to sections G/H):

1. THREE TABLES HAVE RLS DISABLED AND ARE FULLY GRANTED TO anon. `_perm_backup_220` (60 rows: user_id, module_grants), `_purged_visibility_overrides_187` (30 rows: user_id, legacy_scope, visibility_scopes, purged_at), `access_cascade_edges` (609 rows: parent_key, child_key). relrowsecurity=false, and information_schema.role_table_grants shows anon holding SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE on all three. This is the same shape as H1/H2 but through the table door rather than a SECURITY DEFINER function: an unauthenticated caller with the bundled publishable key can read a snapshot of who holds which grants, and can WRITE to the live cascade-edge table. I did not attempt any write. This is the most probe-worthy item in this recon. (The five `_rbac_backup_*` / `permission_grant_archive` tables are the safe pattern: RLS on, zero policies, deny-all.)

2. 32 TABLES ARE `SELECT USING true` FOR authenticated — no grant gates read at all, including `users` (the whole directory), `permission_overrides`-adjacent `access_profiles`, `routing_rules`, `bank_accounts`, `company_settings`, `catalog_items`, `evoucher_history`, `contract_*`, `teams`, `team_memberships`.

3. 11 TABLES ARE `ALL USING true WITH CHECK true` FOR authenticated — fully ungated read AND write: bank_accounts, booking_attachments, booking_milestones, counters, credit_terms, currencies, kpi_definitions, kpi_periods, kpi_scores, settings, user_targets. Any logged-in user can rewrite bank accounts, currencies, counters and every KPI score. `kpi_can_read_others()`/`kpi_can_evaluate()` exist but are referenced by NO policy — and both contain `auth.uid() IS NULL OR ...`, i.e. they return TRUE for an anonymous caller. Dead today, a live bypass the moment anyone wires them into a policy or an RPC.

4. FOUR TABLES ACCEPT `INSERT WITH CHECK true`: activity_log, comments, evoucher_history, tickets. Any authenticated user can forge an audit-log row, a comment, an e-voucher history entry, or a ticket.

5. A `:view` GRANT IS A WRITE GRANT ON FOUR TABLES. projects (UPDATE and DELETE gated on bd/pricing/ops/acct_projects:view), transactions (acct_financials:view / acct_journal:view), memos (exec_memos:view), financial_statement_filings (acct_statements:view). The matching :edit/:delete keys are never checked on those tables. This is not the E15 shape — it is the opposite failure: the grant is present but far too weak.

6. WITH CHECK IS WEAKER THAN USING IN SEVEN PLACES. catalog_categories/catalog_items/category_templates (U), contract_rate_versions (U), exchange_rates (U), memos (U), project_bookings (U), projects (U), transactions (U), financial_statement_filings (U) all have `WITH CHECK true` while USING is gated — so an UPDATE can move a row to any value once the row is visible. On `evouchers` the UPDATE WITH CHECK drops both the `current_user_can_view_record` conjunct and the `status = 'pending_manager'` conjunct that the USING side carries; the reason this is not exploitable today is the BEFORE UPDATE trigger `guard_evoucher_status_change` (migration 270), not the policy.

7. `users` UPDATE has an ungated self-branch: `USING (auth_id = auth.uid()) WITH CHECK (auth_id = auth.uid())`, with NO column restriction. `users.department`, `users.role`, `users.team_id` and `users.access_profile_id` are all inputs to the visibility dial and to the department-string checks below — so a user updating their own row can change the inputs to their own authorization. I did NOT test this; it is a read of the policy text only, and a column-level GRANT or a trigger could still block it. Worth a probe.

8. DEPARTMENT STRINGS ARE STILL LOAD-BEARING IN POLICIES (the H4 shape, in RLS rather than in a function): `users.department <> 'HR'` gates SELECT on 31 profiling/reference tables; `users.department IN ('Accounting','Executive')` gates liquidation_submissions SELECT; `users.department = 'Accounting'` is the ONLY gate on liquidation_submissions UPDATE; `is_executive()` and `is_invoice_approver_of()` are department comparisons. None of these are grant keys, so no grant edit can change them.

9. `evoucher_line_items` has NO grant key on any of its four commands — all four are `EXISTS(evouchers ev WHERE ev.id = evoucher_id)`. Anyone who can see the parent voucher can insert, edit or delete its lines. Same for the whole *_attachments family (contact/customer/project/quotation), contract_attachments, contract_bookings.

10. `memos` SELECT is `is_published` alone — every authenticated user reads every published memo, no grant, no dial, no department.

11. THREE OVERLOADS of current_user_can_view_booking coexist. `bookings` uses the 7-arg version (confidential veto, team via bookings.team_id, booking_assignments). `project_bookings` uses the 5-arg version, which has neither the confidential check nor the booking_assignments path. The generator must not assume "booking visibility" is one function.

12. `current_user_effective_module_grant` reads ONLY `permission_overrides.module_grants`. It never consults access_profiles. This matches the memory note that applying a profile MATERIALIZES grants; a user whose grants were never materialized has zero module permissions in the database no matter what profile label they carry. The dial (`current_user_visibility_dial`) DOES fall back to access_profiles.visibility_scopes when the override is absent — so grants and dials resolve through different paths.

WHAT I COULD NOT DETERMINE.
- I did not enumerate which grant keys actually EXIST in `permission_overrides.module_grants` for real dev users, so I cannot say which of the helper key lists are populated vs. dead (B1 pruned 8,849 dead keys; some of the tab keys above may be among them).
- I did not verify column-level GRANTs; item 7 (users self-update) is a policy reading, not a proven capability.
- I did not read triggers other than confirming the documented `guard_evoucher_status_change` behaviour from the existing harness comments — there may be other non-policy write gates (like that one) that make a policy look looser than the system actually is. Any cell marked predictable=true is predictable *from the policies*; a trigger could still refuse it.
- I checked DEV only. Prod was not touched, per instruction, so I cannot say whether items 1–4 also hold on prod — item 1 in particular should be confirmed there before it is treated as dev-only debris.

states.notes:
SCOPE / METHOD. Everything below was read from the DEV database (oqermaidggvanahumjmj) via read-only SELECTs on information_schema, pg_constraint, pg_trigger, pg_policy and pg_proc, plus greps of src/. No writes. The supabase-prod tools were never called.

1) THE ONE GUARD. public.evouchers is the ONLY table in the schema with a status transition guard. I enumerated every non-internal trigger on all status-bearing tables: the only status-aware ones are evoucher_guard_status (guard_evoucher_status_change), evoucher_enforce_disburse and evoucher_enforce_liquidation_verify — all on evouchers. Every other table's status is a plain text column governed only by an RLS UPDATE policy that asks WHO you are and never WHERE the record is. That is the direct answer to question 4.

2) LIVE FUNCTION == MIGRATION 270. I pulled pg_proc.prosrc for evoucher_transition and compared it against src/supabase/migrations/270_evoucher_transition_guard.sql. They are identical — the matrix transcribed above is the LIVE function, not just the file. prosecdef=true, search_path='public', EXECUTE revoked from public and granted to authenticated. The app is on it too: 11 call sites across 7 files, no remaining raw status writes to evouchers in src/.

3) THREE HOLES INSIDE THE DECLARED MATRIX worth generating probes for:
   (a) The credited/refunded branch has NO from-state restriction. Anyone holding acct_evouchers:edit can move a voucher from ANY status — including 'posted' and 'disbursed', i.e. after cash moved — straight to 'credited' or 'refunded'. Every other branch pins v_from; this one does not.
   (b) 'rejected' is a legal from-state on the cancel branch but NO edge writes 'rejected'. Unreachable through the RPC; live data confirms zero rows carry it.
   (c) The guard trigger is inert when auth.uid() IS NULL. Intentional (service role / seeds / clones), documented in the migration header — but it means a service-role key writes status freely.

4) THE THREE SOURCES DISAGREE, per table:
   - evouchers: 26 values in the TS union (src/types/evoucher.ts), 9 in live data, 13 distinct in the matrix, 0 in constraints. Live data carries "Approved" (1 row, capitalised legacy) for which the matrix has no edge at all — a row in a state the state machine cannot move out of except via the unconstrained credited/refunded branch.
   - invoices: live data carries "Issued" (capital I, 4 rows) while every code path writes lowercase. There is NO InvoiceStatus TS union anywhere — I grepped src/types and src/utils and found only string literals. The codeValues I listed for invoices are harvested literals, NOT a declared type. Do not treat them as authoritative.
   - collections: same — no CollectionStatus type exists. Values harvested from literals in collectionResolution.ts and CollectionDetailsSheet.tsx. Live data has only "posted" and "credited". Column default is 'pending', which nothing in the app ever writes.
   - quotations: TS union has "Needs Revision"; live data has none of it. Otherwise live matches the union.
   - bookings: TS ExecutionStatus has 19 values; SERVICE_STATUS_OPTIONS (the per-service client whitelist) never offers "Created", yet 127 of 239 live bookings ARE "Created" — that value is written on insert, not through the selector. So the selector's whitelist is not even a description of the live vocabulary, let alone an enforcement of it.

5) CHECK CONSTRAINTS ON STATUS exist on exactly six columns in the whole public schema, and none of them is a workflow table: bookings.billing_status (unbilled|billed|partial), calendar_event_participants.status, financial_statement_filings.status, kpi_periods.status, liquidation_submissions.status (pending|approved|revision_requested), tickets.status. evouchers, invoices, collections, bookings.status, quotations and billing_line_items have NO status CHECK at all — hence every constraintValues array above is empty except bookings.billing_status.

6) THE ONE OTHER SERVER-SIDE GATE. approve_invoice(p_invoice_id) is SECURITY DEFINER and re-checks the materialized approver, raising on mismatch (adversary C1 confirms it holds). But it guards approval_status only, and NOT exclusively — invoices_update lets an invoices:edit holder write approval_status directly and I found no trigger preventing that. The generator should probe raw approval_status writes as well as the RPC. Only four SECURITY DEFINER functions in the schema update a workflow table's status at all: approve_invoice, evoucher_transition, send_billing_items_to_booking, repoint_live_bookings_to_rate_version.

7) WHAT I DID NOT VERIFY — do not build probes on these without a second pass. I did not trace app writers or TS constants for expenses.status, transactions.status, budget_requests.status, customers.status, users.status or tasks.status. I DID confirm from pg_trigger that none has a status guard (so they belong in unguardedTables) and I read their live distinct values, but their writers are unmapped. Also: users has trg_guard_user_privileged_columns, and I did not read that function's body — I cannot say whether `status` is one of the columns it protects, so do not assume it is unguarded or guarded either way.

probes.name: send_billing_items_to_booking across customers via the NULL project_id skip
probes.attack: As Accounting/Pricing/BD (a legitimately granted caller — this needs no privilege escalation), call rpc send_billing_items_to_booking with p_booking_id = a booking belonging to CUSTOMER A and p_project_number = a real project_number belonging to CUSTOMER B, plus one virtual item. The function DOES contain a same-tenant guard, but it reads: IF v_booking_project_id IS NOT NULL AND v_booking_project_id <> v_project_id THEN RAISE. Booking A's project_id is NULL for 230 of 239 dev bookings, so the AND short-circuits and the guard never fires. Positive control: repeat with one of the 9 bookings that DOES have project_id set and confirm it raises.
probes.expectedDamage: Revenue lands on the wrong client's project with RLS switched off (SECURITY DEFINER). This is the same NULL-swallows-the-guard shape as H2, in a function that was hardened by migration 271 and still carries the flaw one line lower down. Highest rank because it is a sanctioned entry point, reachable by an ordinary authorised user, and it writes money.

probes.name: Direct billing line whose booking and project_number belong to different customers
probes.attack: As Accounting, plain PostgREST insert into billing_line_items: booking_id = customer A's booking, project_number = customer B's project number, customer_name = customer C's name, amount 250000. Then re-read with service-role eyes and confirm all three disagree.
probes.expectedDamage: BREACH expected. The RPC path at least tries to check; the table path does not check at all — billing_line_items has exactly one CHECK constraint (amount >= 0) and one trigger (updated_at). Revenue attaches to the wrong job, and because 13 rows in live dev data ALREADY have customer_name disagreeing with their booking, this is not hypothetical drift — it is drift that has already happened by ordinary use.

probes.name: Billable e-voucher on a foreign booking auto-mints revenue there
probes.attack: As the Ops requestor, insert an evoucher with booking_id = a booking belonging to a DIFFERENT customer than the requestor's own job, details->>'is_billable' = true, amount 50000, status pending_accounting (or drive it there through evoucher_transition). Then read billing_line_items where source_type='billable_expense' AND source_id = that evoucher id, with service-role eyes.
probes.expectedDamage: BREACH expected, and it is the nastiest kind: the cross-link PROPAGATES BY ITSELF. Trigger trg_ensure_billable_expense_billing_on_approval fires ensure_billable_expense_billing_item(), which is SECURITY DEFINER and copies booking_id and project_number straight off the voucher into a new billing_line_items row — bypassing every billings policy, setting no customer_name, and setting NO catalog_item_id. One AP write silently creates a receivable against the wrong client. This path produced 97 of the 172 billing rows on dev, so it is the dominant writer, not an edge case.

probes.name: E-voucher line item charging a booking its parent voucher has nothing to do with
probes.attack: As the Ops requestor who owns evoucher EV (booking A), insert an evoucher_line_items row with evoucher_id = EV but booking_id = customer B's booking, catalog_item_id = a real expense catalog item, amount 40000.
probes.expectedDamage: BREACH expected. The RLS policy on this table only asks whether the parent evoucher is visible; booking_id is unexamined by policy, constraint and trigger alike. Cost lands on the wrong client's job P&L while the voucher header still reads correctly, so the mismatch is invisible from the voucher screen. Currently 0/273 live rows diverge from their parent — proving the hole is open before anyone falls into it.

probes.name: Attach an unbilled charge to another customer's invoice
probes.attack: As Accounting, UPDATE billing_line_items SET invoice_id = <invoice belonging to CUSTOMER B> WHERE id = <line whose booking_id belongs to CUSTOMER A>. Then read the invoice's line set back and confirm it now contains customer A's charge.
probes.expectedDamage: BREACH expected — no constraint or trigger relates a line's booking/customer to its invoice's. Customer B is literally billed for customer A's work. Combine with the known G4 (an unapproved invoice can be posted) and the wrong-customer invoice can be issued without any approver ever seeing it.

probes.name: Cash receipt applied to a customer that is not the invoice's
probes.attack: As Treasury, insert a collections row with invoice_id = customer A's invoice but customer_name / customer_id = customer B, project_number = a third value, booking_id left NULL (which matches how all 5 live rows are actually written).
probes.expectedDamage: BREACH expected. This is G6's neighbour: G6 covers the AMOUNT being wrong, this covers the PAYER being wrong. Customer B's ledger is credited for money that settles customer A's invoice, so both AR ledgers are wrong in opposite directions and the totals still reconcile — the hardest class of error to spot after the fact. Note the sample here is only 5 live rows, so treat live-data conclusions about collections as thin.

probes.name: Re-parent a live booking onto another customer's project
probes.attack: As a user with booking edit rights, UPDATE bookings SET project_id = <project owned by CUSTOMER B>, and separately UPDATE bookings SET customer_name = 'SOMEONE ELSE' while leaving customer_id pointing at the original customer.
probes.expectedDamage: BREACH expected for both halves. Nothing compares bookings.customer_id to projects.customer_id, and no trigger keeps customer_id and customer_name in step (trg_conf_enforce guards the confidentiality flag only). This moves the ENTIRE job — every billing line, voucher, invoice and collection hanging off it — under the wrong client in one statement, and it is also the only way to make the probe-1 guard fire or not fire at will.

probes.name: Invoice header naming a different customer than its booking
probes.attack: As Accounting, insert an invoice with booking_id = customer A's booking but customer_name and customer_id = customer B; also try the multi-booking form, booking_ids = [customer A's booking, customer B's booking].
probes.expectedDamage: BREACH expected. invoices_insert is a bare create-grant check. The single-booking form produces a document addressed to the wrong party; the booking_ids array form is the more interesting one because 0 live rows use more than one booking, so multi-booking invoicing is entirely UNEXERCISED — a probe here is characterising virgin territory, not confirming a known state.

probes.name: project_number as arbitrary free text
probes.attack: Insert billing lines with project_number set to (a) a project number belonging to another customer, (b) an empty string, (c) 'ANYTHING AT ALL'. Do the same on evouchers.
probes.expectedDamage: BREACH expected on all three, and it should be recorded as characterising a column that is ALREADY broken rather than as a new hole: there is no FK, 170/172 live billing values and 249/249 live evoucher values do not resolve against projects.project_number, 87 are the empty string, and the values that do exist are booking numbers in the wrong namespace. Damage is to reporting and project-level P&L rollups rather than to a single client's money — hence ranked below the ones that move amounts. projects.project_number does carry a UNIQUE index, so an FK here is available as a fix.

probes.name: Booking citing another customer's contract
probes.attack: UPDATE bookings SET contract_id = <a quotation of quotation_type 'contract' belonging to CUSTOMER B> for a booking of customer A; then check what rate_version_id / get_contract_for_booking() returns for it.
probes.expectedDamage: BREACH expected on the write. Damage is indirect but real — contract rates are the basis of the rate snapshot, so customer A's job can be priced off customer B's negotiated contract. Ranked last of the concrete probes because I did NOT verify how far the wrong contract actually propagates into pricing; the write is confirmed unguarded, the downstream effect is inferred.

fks.notes:
WHAT I ACTUALLY VERIFIED, AND WHAT I DID NOT — read this before trusting any row above.

Everything is from the DEV project oqermaidggvanahumjmj, read-only, via SELECT. I ran no writes anywhere and did not touch supabase-prod. Prod may differ; nothing here has been checked against it.

THE HEADLINE. Tenancy is not a security boundary in this system at all — it is only a data-integrity convention, and the convention is enforced in exactly one place. I read every RLS policy on billing_line_items, evouchers, evoucher_line_items, invoices and collections, plus current_user_can_view_record(). Not one of them mentions a customer, a project or a booking. The visibility dial resolves to everything / org_wide / own / team / department and compares an OWNER user id — so 'can I see this row' is answered by who created it and what department they are in, never by whose money it is. There is no policy anywhere that would stop a legitimately-granted Accounting user from touching another customer's financial rows, because from RLS's point of view customers do not exist.

THE ONE PLACE SOMETHING IS CHECKED, AND WHY IT FAILS. send_billing_items_to_booking() resolves p_project_number to a project and then does: IF v_booking_project_id IS NOT NULL AND v_booking_project_id <> v_project_id THEN RAISE. That is a real same-tenant check. It is defeated by bookings.project_id being NULL on 230 of 239 bookings, so for 96% of the estate the guard is a no-op. This is the identical failure shape as finding H2 (NULL NOT IN (...) evaluating to NULL) sitting a dozen lines below the H2 fix, in the same function that migration 271 hardened. Probe 1 is that.

WHERE THE APP AND THE DATABASE DISAGREE — this one will bite whoever writes the probes. CLAUDE.md and the harness fixture both treat project_number as the project's identifier (the fixture writes PROJECT_NUMBER = 'PRJ-ADV-nnnnnn' onto billing_line_items and evouchers, matching projects.project_number). THE DATABASE SAYS OTHERWISE: of 249 evouchers with a project_number, 249 fail to resolve against projects.project_number, and of 172 billing lines, 170 fail. The live values are booking numbers — 'BR202606-003' — while projects.project_number is 'PRJ-869490'. So on real data project_number is a denormalised BOOKING number in a column named for projects, with no FK. APP = project identifier; DATABASE = booking number, unvalidated free text. A probe that asserts a project_number mismatch is 'cosmetic' is testing the harness's own convention, not the system's behaviour — which is why probe 9 is written to characterise the column rather than to prove a rule.

THE DEAD FK COLUMNS. billing_line_items.project_id, evouchers.project_id, evouchers.customer_id, invoices.project_id and collections.project_id all have proper foreign keys and all are populated on ZERO rows. The schema's intended tenancy links exist and are unused; the columns that carry the real link (booking_id, and the text project_number) are respectively FK'd-but-unchecked-for-tenancy and not FK'd at all. Any fix proposal should start here — the plumbing is already laid.

DRIFT THAT HAS ALREADY HAPPENED. 13 of the 72 billing_line_items rows that have a customer_name disagree with the customer_name on the booking they point at. Nobody attacked this system to produce those; ordinary use did. I did NOT determine which surface wrote them or whether they are a rename artefact versus a genuine mis-link — worth a follow-up, and it means probe 2 is reproducing an existing failure mode rather than inventing one.

AN UNEXPECTED ONE, WORTH FLAGGING SEPARATELY. ensure_billable_expense_billing_item() is SECURITY DEFINER, wrote 97 of the 172 billing rows on dev, and inserts with NO catalog_item_id and no customer_name. Finding G5 records catalog doctrine as 'a form convention, not a constraint' and probes it by hand — but the system's own dominant billing writer violates it on every row. G5 is broader than it currently reads. Overall catalog_item_id is NULL on 125/172 billing lines and 72/273 e-voucher lines.

SAMPLE-SIZE CAVEATS, stated so a thin row does not get read as a strong one. invoices = 12 rows, collections = 5 rows. Statements like 'currently 0 invoices disagree with their booking's customer' are true but nearly meaningless at that volume — read them as UNEXERCISED, not as PROTECTED. Multi-booking invoices (booking_ids array) and multi-booking collections are used by 0 rows, so the cross-customer multi-booking case has never run in anger. expenses is 0 rows and orphaned; do not probe it.

WHAT I DID NOT DETERMINE, explicitly. (1) The GL end — transactions and the journal tables. I mapped transactions.evoucher_id and stopped; I did not read its RLS, its own booking/project columns, or whether a cross-linked voucher carries the wrong tenancy into a posted journal entry. That is the single biggest gap in this map and the obvious next recon pass, because damage that reaches the GL is damage that survives. (2) collections has BOTH customer_id and customer_id_alt; I did not establish which the app writes or which reports read. (3) For probe 10 I confirmed the write is unguarded but did not trace how far a foreign contract_id actually propagates into rate snapshots. (4) I did not check whether any of this differs on prod.

fields.decides: Which department's manager may APPROVE or REJECT the voucher. It is the COALESCE fallback for the approver department when pending_approver_department is NULL: the insert trigger copies it into pending_approver_department, and both the RLS approve branch and evoucher_transition's manager edge compare COALESCE(pending_approver_department, details->>'requestor_department') to get_my_department(). It also gates who can READ the pending voucher (evouchers_select same COALESCE).
fields.writableBy: The voucher OWNER: evouchers_update owner branch is (created_by = get_my_profile_id() AND my_evouchers:edit AND can_view_record). No trigger guards the details column (only status is guarded by guard_evoucher_status_change), so the owner may rewrite details freely on their own row at any status. Also fully attacker-controlled at INSERT — the client supplies details, and evouchers_insert only checks my_evouchers:create.

fields.path: pending_approver_department (plain column — the materialized twin of details->>'requestor_department')
fields.decides: The primary decider of which department may approve. Non-null on 262/263 dev rows, so it normally wins the COALESCE over the JSONB fallback — meaning to exploit the JSONB path the attacker must first null this out, which the owner can also do.
fields.writableBy: Same owner branch as details — plain column, not trigger-guarded, so the owner can overwrite the routing target directly (redundant with the JSONB route but simpler).

readBy: RLS evouchers_update (grants FULL UPDATE — top-level OR in BOTH qual and with_check)
fields.decides: A skeleton key on the voucher row. Whoever's profile id equals details->>'cash_receiver_id' gets: (a) read visibility of the voucher, (b) UPDATE on every column of the row except status (the cash_receiver OR-branch has no column restriction and appears in with_check too, so it is self-perpetuating), (c) the right to walk the liquidation transition — i.e. declare how disbursed cash-advance money was spent, and (d) read access to the liquidation submissions.
fields.writableBy: The OWNER (owner branch, details not guarded) may name any profile id as cash_receiver at any status, including after disbursement. The current cash_receiver may also rewrite details (their with_check branch stays satisfied as long as they keep themselves receiver).

fields.decides: Whether an expense e-voucher AUTO-CREATES a customer-facing billing_line_item (revenue) on the linked booking when it reaches pending_accounting/disbursed/posted. The trigger fires on details change too, and the SECDEF insert bypasses billing RLS and writes with NO catalog_item_id (also trips G5).
fields.writableBy: The owner (owner branch; details not guarded) can flip is_billable on their own voucher, or set it at INSERT.

fields.decides: Whether a demurrage/detention charge is auto-proposed as 'internal' fault (blame the company vs the customer) in the KPI engine. Lower impact — advisory proposal, not an enforced permission.
fields.writableBy: Anyone who can UPDATE the booking (current_user_can_act_on_booking('edit') on a visible booking).

fields.decides: Only a usage COUNT of how many bookings reference an assignment profile — informational, no security/routing decision. Included for completeness; not a tamper target.

probes.name: requestor steers her own voucher to a friendly approver via details.requestor_department
probes.tamper: As the owner (Ops TL, my_evouchers:edit), UPDATE her own pending_manager voucher: set details = jsonb_set(details,'{requestor_department}','"Operations"') and set pending_approver_department = NULL. Both are permitted by the evouchers_update owner branch and neither column is trigger-guarded (only status is). The insert-trigger/COALESCE fallback then makes 'Operations' the approver department.
probes.gain: Defeats the arm's-length routing rule (Forwarding-job expenses -> Pricing Manager, routing_rules priority 10) that exists precisely so the requestor's own boss does not approve her spend. After the tamper, evoucher_transition's manager edge accepts opsMgr (Mariella, Operations, holds my_evouchers:approve) — her own manager rubber-stamps the voucher that was supposed to go to Pricing. Operations has 3 approvers to choose from; a requestor can route to whichever department has a colluding manager.

probes.name: owner names an arbitrary cash_receiver_id to hand out a full-update + liquidation skeleton key
probes.tamper: As owner, UPDATE the voucher setting details->>'cash_receiver_id' to an accomplice's profile id (or her own). The evouchers_update owner branch allows the write; details is not guarded.
probes.gain: The named id instantly gains, on that voucher: read visibility, UPDATE of every column except status (the cash_receiver OR-branch is in qual AND with_check, unrestricted by column), and the right to walk the liquidation transition — i.e. to declare how the disbursed cash was spent. This breaks segregation of duties: the requestor can appoint herself both requestor and cash-receiver/liquidator, or appoint an accomplice who alters amount/vendor/bank details after disbursement. A named receiver can also keep the key alive indefinitely (with_check stays satisfied while cash_receiver_id = self).

probes.name: owner flips details.is_billable to inject a catalog-less revenue line onto a customer booking
probes.tamper: As owner, UPDATE the booking-linked expense voucher setting details->>'is_billable' = 'true' (or set it at INSERT). The AFTER trigger ensure_billable_expense_billing_item_on_approval fires on the details change once status is >= pending_accounting.
probes.gain: The SECURITY DEFINER ensure_billable_expense_billing_item() inserts a billing_line_item (customer-facing revenue) on the linked booking, bypassing the billings RLS (INSERT check current_user_can_billings) entirely and writing with catalog_item_id NULL (also violates catalog doctrine, G5). A user with no billings grant thus plants an arbitrary billable charge on a customer's booking through the expense side.

probes.name: booking editor sets details.det_dem_validity to swing KPI fault attribution
probes.tamper: UPDATE a visible booking's details->>'det_dem_validity' to a late date so empty_returned no longer exceeds validity.
probes.gain: Suppresses kpi_propose_fault's 'internal' (company-at-fault) proposal for demurrage/detention charges, shifting suggested blame off the company. Advisory only (the function proposes, a human decides), so low severity — listed for completeness.

jsonb.notes:
Scope: dev project oqermaidggvanahumjmj, read-only, verified against the live database (pg_policies, pg_get_functiondef, pg_trigger), not inferred from app code. Grants read from permission_overrides.

WHERE APP AND DB DISAGREE: none of these decisions is enforced in the UI form path — the app never offers these edits — but PostgREST accepts them because the RLS owner branch on evouchers_update places no column restriction and only the `status` column carries a guard trigger (guard_evoucher_status_change, migration 270). Every other column of a voucher the caller owns — including the JSONB `details` — is freely writable by the owner while the row is theirs and visible.

THE STRUCTURAL HOLE (one sentence): migration 270 correctly closed `status` behind evoucher_transition(), but the SAME row carries `details` (requestor_department, cash_receiver_id, is_billable) and `pending_approver_department`, and those are the inputs the approval routing, the read policy, and the liquidation edge trust — all still owner-writable. Closing status without freezing the fields that decide status's route is a lock on the door beside an open window.

requestor_department caveat (verified): pending_approver_department is non-null on 262/263 dev rows, so the COALESCE normally reads the materialized column, not the JSONB. The JSONB fallback bites when the attacker first nulls pending_approver_department (owner can) OR inserts a voucher that matches no routing_rule. Only one routing_rule exists for domain 'evoucher' (Forwarding -> Pricing), so any non-Forwarding expense already falls through to the requestor_department fallback with no tampering at all.

cash_receiver_id bootstrap caveat: a stranger cannot self-name (qual's cash_receiver branch requires already being the receiver); the write must originate from the owner branch or an existing receiver. So the attack is owner-appoints-accomplice or receiver-retains-control, not arbitrary self-elevation.

NOT a hole: bookings.details->'profile_refs' (usage count only) and quotations.details->'contract_general_details' (read by detect_active_contracts_for_customer, which gates on current_user_can_detect_contracts and returns rows, not permissions).

fixtures.notes:
VERIFIED AGAINST THE LIVE DEV DATABASE (oqermaidggvanahumjmj) VIA information_schema.columns, pg_constraint, pg_trigger + pg_get_functiondef, pg_policy, and SELECTs against real rows. Nothing was inserted, updated or deleted. supabase-prod was never touched.

THE HEADLINE, AND THE GOOD NEWS FOR THE HARNESS: this schema is extremely permissive. Across all 15 tables there are only SIX NOT NULL columns without a usable default — bookings.service_type, tickets.subject, tickets.type, tickets.created_by, customers.name, catalog_categories.name/side, catalog_items.name, service_providers.provider_type/company_name, users.name — plus every table's `id`. There are only SIX CHECK constraints that can realistically bite (tickets x5, catalog_categories.side, users x3, bookings.billing_status, catalog_items.kpi_charge_class, evoucher_line_items.fault_class), and almost all of them pass on NULL. Status columns are NOT constrained anywhere except tickets: quotations, projects, bookings, evouchers, invoices, collections and expenses all accept ANY string as status. That means a probe that fails is overwhelmingly likely to be failing on permissions, which is exactly what the matrix wants.

THE FOUR WAYS A PROBE CAN STILL DIE ON A CONSTRAINT RATHER THAN A PERMISSION — these are the failure mode you asked me to prevent:
1. catalog_categories: the column DEFAULT is 'both' and the CHECK only allows 'revenue'|'expense'. Omitting `side` is a guaranteed 23514. Always pass it.
2. tickets.created_by: NOT NULL, FK to users(id), and there is NO stamping trigger on this table (unlike bookings/evouchers/invoices/collections/expenses/quotations). Must be a real users.id.
3. UNIQUE columns: invoices.invoice_number and projects.project_number. Two parallel probe runs with the same stamp collide and the second reads as 23505, not as a denial.
4. base_currency: five tables (billing_line_items, collections, evouchers, expenses, invoices) have base_currency NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PHP' with an FK to currencies(code). 'PHP' exists, so OMIT the column. Setting it to anything not in `currencies` raises an FK error.

ID CONVENTIONS ARE GENUINELY MIXED — DO NOT ASSUME UUID. Only ONE table in the set has a working id default (evoucher_line_items, gen_random_uuid()::text) and ONE has a real uuid PK type (tickets, gen_random_uuid()). Every other table requires the caller to supply the id string. Live conventions: quotations QUO-<ms>, projects proj-<ms>, bookings bare uuid (text column), evouchers evoucher-<ms>-<rand>, billing_line_items uuid OR BIL-<ms>-<rand> (both live), invoices uuid, collections uuid, customers CUST-<ms>, service_providers sp-<ms> (app) / np-* (seed), catalog_items ci-<ms>, catalog_categories cat-<ms>, users user-<hex8>. expenses is EMPTY so its convention is UNDETERMINED — I am flagging that rather than guessing.

APP-vs-DB DISAGREEMENTS I FOUND (both reported, DB is authoritative):
- quotations.quotation_type: DB default is 'standard'; live data and the app only ever use 'spot'|'contract'|'project'. There is no CHECK, so 'standard' would be accepted and would be invisible to every app filter.
- catalog doctrine (CLAUDE.md: "no line-item insert may omit catalog_item_id"): the DB has catalog_item_id NULLABLE with no check on billing_line_items, evoucher_line_items AND expenses. This is the app rule with no DB counterpart — already recorded as finding G5 / probes A8 and D1.
- invoice approval gate: no trigger or constraint on invoices enforces approval_status before status='posted'. Client-only — finding G4 / probe C2.
- collections has no relationship whatsoever to the invoice balance — finding G6 / probe C5.

TWO INSERT-TIME SIDE EFFECTS THE FIXTURE MUST PLAN FOR (both AFTER INSERT, both SECURITY DEFINER):
- evouchers.trg_ensure_billable_expense_billing_on_approval: seeding a voucher at pending_accounting/disbursed/pending_liquidation/pending_verification/posted WITH details.is_billable=true AND a booking_id will CREATE a billing_line_items row. The current adversary fixture escapes this only because it never sets is_billable.
- bookings.trg_capture_booking_milestones: passing a `details` object containing any key listed in booking_milestone_sources creates booking_milestones rows keyed 'bm-<booking_id>-<key>'. Teardown does not currently delete these.

ONE MORE THING WORTH A PROBE (found while reading the insert policies, not asked for): two RLS INSERT policies are effectively open. tickets_insert has WITH CHECK (true) — any authenticated caller can create a ticket attributed to any users.id. evoucher_line_items_insert only checks that the parent voucher EXISTS — any authenticated caller can append a line, and therefore an amount, to ANY e-voucher in the system regardless of status, owner or department. Neither is in sections G or H of findings.md.

WHAT I COULD NOT DETERMINE:
- expenses id convention and status vocabulary (zero rows, no app writer).
- The body of guard_customer_delete() — I confirmed the BEFORE DELETE trigger exists on customers but did not read it, so I cannot say which references block a fixture customer teardown.
- I did not enumerate UPDATE/SELECT/DELETE policies; only INSERT policies, since the question was about valid insert payloads. The insert WITH CHECK expressions are listed per table above so the matrix knows which grant each insert probe is actually testing.

METHOD. Everything above came from SELECTs against dev (oqermaidggvanahumjmj) via the supabase MCP tools — public.users joined to public.permission_overrides, plus auth.users, public.access_profiles, public.team_memberships, pg_proc and pg_policy. No writes, no prod. Repo reading was limited to tests/e2e/adversary.spec.ts and the heading index of docs/qa/findings.md.

THE TWO DIALS, AS THE DATABASE ACTUALLY IMPLEMENTS THEM.

1. module_grants is NOT {module: [actions]}. It is a FLAT jsonb object keyed "module:action" -> boolean, e.g. {"inbox:view": true, "acct_evouchers:disburse": true}. Values can be explicitly false, which is not the same as absent — wenchemaes@ carries "acct_evouchers:approve": false. Counting jsonb keys therefore overstates authority; every count in this report is of keys whose value is literally true. Two users on the roster have false-valued keys (wenchemaes 1, and several others outside the roster carry up to 174).

2. visibility_scopes is {record_type: 'own'|'team'|'org_wide'|'everything'} over 21 record types. Resolution order in current_user_visibility_dial(p_record_type) is: the user's own override -> the user's active access_profile -> 'own'. A missing key is NOT 'everything'; it silently becomes the profile's value or 'own'. Ten of the twelve roster members declare all 21 keys in the override; jr.cusdec01 declares 7 and treasury@/wenchemaes@/accountreceivables@ declare 14, so those four are the only rows that exercise the fallback path. Effective (post-fallback) dials are what I reported, not raw override contents.

3. The two dials are genuinely independent and the roster proves it. hrmanager@ has 7 grants but 'everything' on bookings_forwarding. accountreceivables@ (staff) has 313 grants — more than either Accounting manager — and org_wide on everything, but no AP authority. inquiry@ has 663 grants and 'everything' on all 21 types yet does NOT hold acct_evouchers:disburse. A probe that only varies one dial will misattribute its result.

WHERE APP AND DATABASE DISAGREE.
- Role tiers: CLAUDE.md / project memory describe Staff/TL/Manager/Executive. The DATABASE has only staff/team_leader/manager, with Executive as a department. Database wins for probe construction.
- Teams: users.team_id is NULL for all 60 rows (the app-facing column), while team_memberships has 51 active rows and is what current_user_team_ids() reads. Database (team_memberships) wins.
- permission_overrides.scope is written by the app but referenced by no RLS policy. Inert for this matrix.

COMPARABILITY WITH THE EXISTING HARNESS. All five spine/adversary actors are in the roster with the same keys the spec uses: bd=jr.businessdev02, pricingMgr=jr.manager03, ops=jr.supervisor07, opsMgr=jr.manager02, treasury=treasury@.
